The eight problems whose remaining work is days to about a week are now closure programs, ordered smallest first, so each loop runs its quickest one before anything else. The months-long residuals stay in the DAG and aren't dropped. The loops are running. ㊢ (closure programs, in priority order) | Priority | Problem | Loop | Remaining | |---|---|---|---| | 41 | t95J02 | topo1 | quotient-circle homeomorphism, 2–5 days | | 42 | t92J08 | topo1 | uniform Picard–Lindelöf on manifolds, then the last bridge | | 43 | *point-wedge van Kampen* | topo1 | shared by 5 problems (the existing program) | | 43 | t97A04 | topo2 | bridge 3: torus H₂ naturality and degree | | 44 | t97A07 | topo1 | openness of regular points, then the submersion argument | | 45 | t96A07 | topo2 | three derivative calculations | | 46 | t94A10 | topo2 | closedness, then non-exactness via periodic Green | | 47 | t91J06 | topo1 | interval coordinates, then the corrected glue | | 48 | t94A07 | topo1 | torus index and the longitude obstruction | - **First job:** each program writes `ConstructionTargets/

Closure.blueprint.md` from its audit or closer report, then formalises it node by node. - **Stops:** a stop that passes review reopens the program, for up to 10 jobs. - **topo3:** it has no quick problems; it keeps its deck-group program at 50. - **Checks:** all ledgers validate, and the lab tests pass. ㊟ (what this costs) While a loop has a program open, it takes that program before any lemma row the strategy checkpoints elect. So topo1 works mostly in series: t95J02, then t92J08, then van Kampen, and so on. Lemma breadth work slows in topo1 and topo2 until these finish. That's the trade you asked for. I put van Kampen at 43 so the foundation serving five problems isn't held up behind all of topo1's closures. ㊭ ("efficiency enhancements") For the months-long residuals (surface classification, Lefschetz, wild-ball complements, Stokes on manifolds), these could help once the quick ones are under way: - a **Mathlib search** before each blueprint node, since several "missing" pieces turned out to exist in some form; - **reviewed blueprints**, so formalisation jobs don't stop on representation problems; - running the **hardest blueprint nodes on a stronger model seat**, at a higher quota cost per job. 🈳 (t98A02, from my last message) Still your call: whether to add a local-flatness hypothesis to t98A02, or keep the wild-ball version on the long route.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-14
previous_reply_acts.text:
(what's in place)
- **`BLUEPRINTS.md`** in the lab sets out the order and the format: `ConstructionTargets/<Foundation>.blueprint.md`, one node per future Lean declaration, each with `uses:` edges, the intended Lean type, and the Lean representation wherever there's a choice. A node needing more than about a page gets split, and every hypothesis of the final theorem has to be used by some node. Blueprints are only for FOUNDATION-sized theorems; READY and NEAR problems go straight from audit to closure, as t00J08 did.
- **Work prompt:** a program whose blueprint doesn't exist yet writes it as its whole job, commits it, and stops. After that, its milestones are the blueprint's nodes, and a STOP has to name the node it's stuck on. A strategy checkpoint may elect a multi-day foundation row only with a reviewed blueprint behind it; otherwise it elects the blueprint.
- **Review prompt:** blueprints are reviewed for their mathematics. Are the statements true as written, does each proof use only its `uses:` nodes and stated hypotheses, and is each Lean type a faithful form of its statement? A failure has to come with the counterexample or the missing hypothesis.
- **Programs:** van Kampen writes `PointWedgeVanKampen.blueprint.md`, working from the t99J01, t01A03, t01A04, t92J06, t97A01 and t97A03 audits. Deck-group writes `DeckGroupQuotientFundamentalGroup.blueprint.md`, from the t93J03, t00A02, t00J07 and t99J01 audits.
- **Checks:** both ledgers validate and the lab tests pass.
